name: Liechtenstein, bought by a princely family
anchor: Vaduz, the county bought in 1712.
founder: Prince Johann Adam Andreas of Liechtenstein
recognition: Imperial principality from 1719; independent sovereign state from 1806
cost: 115,000 guilders for Schellenberg and 290,000 guilders for Vaduz
story: Liechtenstein, the small country between Switzerland and Austria, began as a purchase. The Liechtenstein family were very rich nobles whose estates lay in Bohemia, Moravia, Silesia and Austria, inside the lands of the Habsburg dynasty. The emperor had made the head of the family an imperial prince in 1620, but only rulers of land directly under the emperor could sit and vote in the Imperial Diet, the assembly of the Holy Roman Empire. The family therefore needed a territory of that kind. The lordship of Schellenberg and the county of Vaduz, in the Alpine Rhine Valley, qualified. They were badly run and in debt under the counts of Hohenems, and an imperial commission decided they should be sold to clear those debts. Prince Johann Adam Andreas outbid the other interested parties and paid 115,000 guilders for Schellenberg, well above its value, with the handover ceremony in 1699. Schellenberg alone was judged too small to earn a seat, so the deal included first refusal on Vaduz, which he bought for 290,000 guilders in 1712. Vaduz's men swore allegiance only after being promised that their old rights would continue. In 1719 Emperor Charles VI joined the two lands into the Principality of Liechtenstein. It became a sovereign state in 1806, when Napoleon's Confederation of the Rhine took it out of the empire. No ruling prince visited until 1842, and the family still reigns there today.
mechanism: A family bought land from an indebted count with the emperor's approval, and the emperor then raised it to a principality. Land and ruling rights both passed because the overlord agreed, and full independence came later through the collapse of the empire around it.

sources.t: How the Principality of Liechtenstein came into being, Swiss National Museum

name: White Rajahs of Sarawak
anchor: Kuching, the town at the centre of the 1841 grant.
stopped_by: Cession to Britain by the third Rajah in 1946
challenge: The heir and most native members of the Council Negri opposed the 1946 cession
recognition: Described as a sovereign state under the Brookes; recognition by other states not confirmed
cost: No price; granted in return for help against piracy and uprisings
story: Sarawak, on the north-west coast of Borneo, was ruled for 105 years by a British family called Brooke. It had been a vassal territory of the Sultanate of Brunei, meaning it owed loyalty to the sultan. In 1841 Sultan Omar Ali Saifuddin II granted James Brooke, a man of British origin born in India, the area around the town of Sarawak (now Kuching) and the nearby Bau mining district, in return for help against piracy and uprisings. Brooke was later confirmed with the title of Rajah. He rebuilt the government on the British model, and he and his successor leased or annexed more land from Brunei until the state covered much of northern Borneo. The title passed down the male line to a nephew and then to his son, Vyner Brooke. After the Japanese occupation in the Second World War, Vyner ceded Sarawak to the British Colonial Office in 1946. Because the legality of that cession was unclear, Britain also passed an annexation bill. His nephew and legal heir, Anthony Brooke, objected, and so did most native members of the Council Negri, the local parliament. A British governor, Duncan Stewart, was assassinated by members of a group seeking union with Indonesia. Sarawak became a British Crown colony and in 1963 a state of Malaysia.
mechanism: A ruler can hand over territory and the right to govern it to a private person as a reward, with no sale price, and the grant holds as long as outside powers accept it. The Brooke family's rule ended when one member transferred it to Britain, over the objection of the heir.

name: British North Borneo Company
anchor: Sandakan, the seat of the company governor.
founder: Gustav von Overbeck and Alfred and Edward Dent
stopped_by: War damage led the company to give up its charter in 1946
cost: 15,000 Spanish dollars to Brunei and 5,000 to Sulu; Britain later paid £860,000 and an arbitrator awarded £1.4 million
story: The British North Borneo Company was a private company that ran what is now Sabah, a state of Malaysia on the island of Borneo, for over 60 years. It began with a deal made by Baron von Overbeck, a German businessman and diplomat, and the brothers Alfred and Edward Dent, who headed a British trading firm in Shanghai and London. They wanted a colonial concession, meaning a grant of rights over the land. In December 1877 the Sultan of Brunei agreed to one for 15,000 Spanish dollars. It then emerged that Brunei had already given some of the area to the Sultan of Sulu, so a second agreement was signed with him in January 1878 for 5,000 Spanish dollars. Overbeck and the Dents thereby became rulers of the territory. Overbeck left in 1879 after failing to interest Germany, and Dent turned to Britain, which sealed a charter for the company in November 1881. The company issued laws, recruited police and set up courts. Britain made the territory a protectorate in 1888, meaning Britain took charge of its foreign relations. The Second World War left the company unable to pay for rebuilding, so it gave North Borneo to the Colonial Office in 1946 for £860,000 in cash, and in 1949 an arbitrator added £1.4 million in compensation. The territory joined Malaysia in 1963.
mechanism: Two local rulers signed away rights over land to private men, and a charter from Britain then gave the company the backing to govern it. Whether the Sulu agreement was a sale or a lease is still disputed.

name: Sulu heirs' $15 billion claim against Malaysia
anchor: Kota Kinabalu, capital of Sabah, the land at issue. The hearings were in Madrid and Paris.
founder: Eight people claiming descent from the Sultan of Sulu
stopped_by: French courts annulled the award
challenge: Malaysia rejected the arbitration; the heirs failed to seize Malaysian assets in France, the Netherlands and Luxembourg
recognition: Malaysia rejects any claim to Sabah
cost: $14.92 billion awarded in 2022, later annulled
story: This is a legal fight over the 1878 deal that handed part of northern Borneo, now the Malaysian state of Sabah, to the private British North Borneo Company. Under that deal the Sultan of Sulu either ceded or leased the land, a point never settled, and the company agreed to pay him and his heirs a yearly fee. Malaysia took over the payments after it was formed in 1963 and stopped them after the 2013 Lahad Datu standoff, an armed incursion into Sabah by followers of a Sulu claimant. Eight people who say they are the sultan's heirs began arbitration in Spain in 2019. Arbitration is a private hearing where an appointed person decides a dispute in place of a court. Malaysia refused to take part, saying the matter belonged in its own courts. A Madrid court annulled the appointment of the arbitrator, Gonzalo Stampa, in 2021, so he moved the case to Paris and in February 2022 ordered Malaysia to pay $14.92 billion. Spanish courts convicted Stampa of contempt of court, and the conviction was upheld on appeal in May 2024. France's highest court ruled against the heirs in November 2024, and in December 2025 Malaysia announced that the Paris Court of Appeal had annulled the whole award because no valid arbitration agreement bound Malaysia. A spokesman for the sultanate said the legal fight was not over.
mechanism: A colonial-era contract can outlive the empire that made it and be used to claim money from the modern state. French courts held that its dispute clause, which named a British consul-general whose post no longer exists, did not bind Malaysia to private arbitration.

sources.t: Malaysia touts court order voiding $14.9-B Sulu claim, Daily Tribune and AFP

name: Leopold II's Congo Free State
anchor: Marker is near the centre of the former state.
founder: King Leopold II of the Belgians
stopped_by: International pressure and annexation by the Belgian Parliament
challenge: The Congo Reform Association campaigned against the regime
recognition: Recognised by the United States in 1884, then France and the Berlin Conference powers
cost: Goods given to local leaders under what were called cloth-and-trinket treaties; no total price is recorded
story: The Congo Free State was a state in Central Africa covering all of what is now the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and it was the private possession of one man, King Leopold II of Belgium. It was not part of Belgium. The two countries only shared a monarch, an arrangement called a personal union. Leopold wanted a colony, so he hired the explorer Henry Morton Stanley. From 1879 to 1884 Stanley built roads and posts in the Congo Basin and signed treaties with local leaders that in effect gave Leopold rights over their land. Leopold grouped these under a body called the International Association of the Congo and presented it as a humanitarian project. In April 1884 the United States became the first country to recognise the association's claim, after a lobbying campaign that used edited copies of the treaties. France followed, on condition that it got the first option to buy the territory if Leopold ever sold. The Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885 then accepted the association under his personal control. Leopold ran the state from Brussels and never visited it. He claimed unoccupied land as state property and granted rubber concessions to companies. Forced labour, torture and murder followed, and the highest estimates put deaths at half the population of the rubber provinces, though poor records make the number uncertain. After an international campaign exposed the abuses, the Belgian Parliament annexed the territory in 1908 as a colony called the Belgian Congo.
mechanism: A private person turned bundles of treaties with local leaders into a state by persuading outside powers to recognise it. Recognition came from those powers. One contemporary account says the local leaders who signed did not understand a word of the treaties.

name: Rudd Concession
anchor: Marker is in Matabeleland. The document names only the king's royal kraal.
founder: Charles Rudd, Rochfort Maguire and Francis Thompson
recognition: A private grant by a king; it does not claim statehood
cost: £100 a lunar month, 1,000 rifles, 100,000 cartridges, and a steamboat or £500, for mineral rights only
story: The Rudd Concession was an 1888 agreement in which King Lobengula of Matabeleland, in what is now Zimbabwe, signed away the mineral rights of his kingdom to three men, Charles Rudd and Francis Thompson of Kimberley and Rochfort Maguire of London. The text promised him £100 every lunar month, 1,000 Martini-Henry rifles with 100,000 cartridges, and either a steamboat with guns on the Zambezi River or £500. In return the three men received complete and exclusive charge over all metals and minerals in his lands, and the power to do whatever they judged necessary to get them. The king also authorised them to keep out everyone else seeking land or mining rights, and agreed to grant no more concessions without their consent. The document says this was because rival concession seekers had been bothering him. A witness named Helm certified that the terms had been explained to the king and his council. The grant was to end if the monthly payment fell three months behind. In the years that followed, Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company held charter lands in the region and was expanding them northward.
mechanism: The written deal covered minerals and the right to exclude rivals. It transferred no sovereignty and no land on its face, which shows how a narrow commercial grant can still shut a ruler out of dealing with anyone else.

sources.t: Rudd Concession by King Lobengula of Matabeleland (1888), South African History Online

name: Clunies-Ross family of the Cocos (Keeling) Islands
anchor: Marker is on the atoll, near Home Island.
recognition: Land grant from the British Crown; never a separate state
cost: A$6.25 million in 1978 for the land and buildings, apart from the family home
story: The Cocos (Keeling) Islands are a small group in the Indian Ocean, now an Australian territory, that one Scottish family owned for about 150 years. The islands were empty until the 1820s, when an Englishman, Alexander Hare, arrived with a party made up mostly of people of Malay origin. Captain John Clunies-Ross, a Scottish seaman, settled in 1827 and began harvesting coconuts. Britain annexed the islands in 1857, and in 1886 Queen Victoria granted all the land to the Clunies-Ross family. Sovereignty stayed with Britain, which ran them as a dependency of its Singapore colony, and in 1955 they became a territory of Australia. The family remained the landowner. In 1978 the Australian government paid A$6.25 million for the family's property, apart from their home, Oceania House, and its grounds on Home Island. In 1984 the Cocos Malay residents voted overwhelmingly to join Australia fully, in a United Nations-supervised vote called an Act of Self Determination. Australia bought the last of John Cecil Clunies-Ross's property in 1993 and sold Oceania House privately in 2001.
mechanism: The family held title to all the land under a grant from the Crown, while Britain and then Australia kept sovereignty. So when the Australian government wanted control it could simply buy the land.

sources.t: Current and future governance arrangements for the Indian Ocean Territories, Parliament of Australia

name: Hudson's Bay Company's sale of Rupert's Land
anchor: Marker is west of Hudson Bay, inside the territory.
stopped_by: Sale to Canada
challenge: The Red River Resistance delayed the transfer until 1870
recognition: British royal charter; sovereignty lay with the Crown
cost: £300,000 (about CAD$1.5 million), with the company keeping its posts and five per cent of the land
story: Rupert's Land was a territory of 3.9 million square kilometres around Hudson Bay, about a third of present-day Canada, that a private company held for 200 years. King Charles II of England gave the Hudson's Bay Company a charter in 1670 with exclusive rights to trade and colonise all land whose rivers drained into the bay. The charter gave almost no thought to the sovereignty of the Cree, Assiniboine and other Indigenous peoples living there. After Canada was formed in 1867, its government wanted the land, partly from fear that the United States, which had just bought Alaska, would take it. The company, for its part, lacked the money to govern a territory that was filling with settlers. It valued the land at up to $40 million, and the United States could have paid that, but Britain would not allow a sale to the Americans and pressed the company to deal with Canada. After six months of talks the company agreed to £300,000, or about $1.5 million, and kept its trading posts and five per cent of the land, mostly prairie farmland. It signed the land over to the British Crown on 19 November 1869, and the Crown ceded it to Canada. The Red River Resistance, a rising by local people, delayed the transfer until 15 July 1870. Canada then negotiated seven treaties with Indigenous nations to obtain their consent to Crown sovereignty.
mechanism: The company could sell only what its charter gave it, so the transfer went through the British Crown to Canada. Indigenous nations were not party to the sale, and Canada made treaties with them afterwards.

name: Lord Selkirk's Red River Colony
anchor: Winnipeg, on the site of the settlement.
challenge: The North West Company fought the colony
recognition: Grant under the Hudson's Bay Company charter
story: The Red River Colony was a settlement scheme around present-day Winnipeg in Canada, on a block of land the size of five Scotlands that a private company gave to one nobleman. Thomas Douglas, Earl of Selkirk, was troubled by the eviction of Scottish farmers in the Highland Clearances and believed emigration was their best hope. He saw that he needed one of the big fur companies on his side. In 1811 the Hudson's Bay Company granted him 300,000 square kilometres out of its own territory, known as the Selkirk Concession or Assiniboia. The company expected the colony to grow food for its fur trade and cut the cost of shipping supplies. Selkirk bought many company shares in 1811 and 1812, and historians have debated how far that explains the grant. The rival North West Company opposed the colony. In 1816 the colony's governor, Robert Semple, and about 20 settlers were killed at the Battle of Seven Oaks, and the settlement was abandoned for a time. Selkirk arrived the next year with about 100 disbanded soldiers and captured the rival's headquarters at Fort William. The land south of the 49th parallel passed to the United States under an 1818 treaty, and the colony existed until 1870, when the Hudson's Bay territory went to Canada.
mechanism: A chartered company could pass part of its territory to a private person, and the grant carried land under the company's charter. It gave no independence from Britain.

name: Palmyra Atoll and the Fullard-Leo family
challenge: The federal government sued to quiet title; the family won at the Supreme Court in 1947
recognition: Private title under United States sovereignty
cost: $15,000 in 1922; $30 million in 2000, for land only
story: Palmyra is an uninhabited coral atoll in the central Pacific, 1,000 miles south of Hawaii, that was bought and sold by private owners while also being claimed by governments. The Kingdom of Hawaii annexed it in 1862 and two Hawaiian citizens became its joint owners. Their shares were then sold and inherited many times. In 1922 Henry Cooper sold his interest to Leslie and Ellen Fullard-Leo for $15,000, and they set up a company to harvest coconuts. The atoll came under the United States when Hawaii did. The family tried from 1937 to lease it to the Navy, but during the talks the federal government sued them, claiming that the atoll had never been lawfully private property, and the Navy occupied it and built a runway during the Second World War. The US Supreme Court ruled for the Fullard-Leo and Cooper families in United States v. Fullard-Leo in 1947, which confirmed their private title against the government. The family later turned down offers to use the atoll as a nuclear waste dump or a casino, according to the Nature Conservancy, a conservation charity, which bought most of the land from them in 2000 for $30 million. Palmyra is now a federal wildlife refuge and the only incorporated US territory, meaning one treated as an integral part of the United States.
mechanism: Owning land and governing it are separate things. The family won clear private title against the federal government in court, yet the atoll stayed under United States sovereignty throughout.

sources.t: Owner's devotion to Palmyra credited with atoll's preservation, Honolulu Star-Bulletin

name: Lundy under Martin Harman
anchor: Marker is on the island.
stopped_by: Prosecution under the Coinage Act 1870
currency: Half Puffin and One Puffin coins, issued 1929 and withdrawn after the 1931 ruling
challenge: Conviction upheld by the High Court in 1931
story: Lundy is a small English island in the Bristol Channel, about 5 kilometres long, which has often been privately owned. The businessman Martin Coles Harman bought it from the Christie family in 1924, along with its mail contract and a boat. In 1929 he issued his own coins, the Half Puffin and the One Puffin, set equal in value to the British halfpenny and penny and named after the puffin, the bird that gave the island its name. Because Lundy was part of England, he was prosecuted under the Coinage Act of 1870. Devon magistrates fined him £5 with £15 15 shillings in costs in April 1930. He appealed to the High Court in 1931 and lost. The coins were withdrawn and became collector's items. The island was bought in 1969 by the millionaire Jack Hayward, who gave it to the National Trust, a British conservation charity. The Landmark Trust now manages it and pays for it through day trips and holiday lets.
mechanism: Buying an island brings title to the land, and the national law continues to apply. Harman's conviction showed that a private owner cannot issue money in a place that remains part of the state.

name: Herm island lease sales
anchor: Marker is on the island.
founder: Successive tenants, most recently Starboard Settlement
recognition: None sought; part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey
cost: £15 million asked in 2008 for the remaining 40-year lease; sold for considerably less
story: Herm is a tiny island in the Channel Islands, about a mile and a half long, part of the Bailiwick of Guernsey, whose right of use has been traded for over a century while the ownership stayed with a government. Prince Gebhard Blücher, a German noble, leased it from the British government in 1889 and brought in wallabies. The novelist Compton Mackenzie took over the tenancy in 1920. The States of Guernsey, the island's government, bought Herm from the Crown in 1949 so that local people and tourists could enjoy it, and let it to Major Peter Wood, who restored the run-down island with his wife over 30 years. In 2008 his daughter and her husband put the remaining 40 years of their lease up for sale, asking £15 million. A trust called Starboard Settlement bought it for considerably less and formed Herm Island Ltd to run the island. Talks on a 21-year extension broke down in 2013, with the tenant offering £440,000 and the owner asking for £6 million. Herm Island Ltd still runs the island.
mechanism: What was sold was a lease, a right to use land for a fixed time. The government of Guernsey kept ownership.

name: Niʻihau and the Robinson family
anchor: Marker is on the island.
recognition: Private land within the US state of Hawaii
cost: $10,000 in gold in 1864, for land only
story: Niʻihau is the seventh largest Hawaiian island, 180 square kilometres, and it has been privately owned by one family since a Scottish plantation owner, Elizabeth Sinclair, bought it from King Kamehameha V of Hawaii in 1864. She paid $10,000 in gold, a price that also covered parts of the island of Kauaʻi. Ownership passed to her descendants, the Robinson family, and brothers Bruce and Keith Robinson now manage it. Hawaii later became part of the United States, and Niʻihau is counted within Kauaʻi County. The family's rules keep the island closed to outsiders apart from relatives, US Navy personnel, officials and invited guests, which has earned it the name the Forbidden Isle and some controversy. Supervised tours and hunting trips have been allowed since 1987. Its residents, mostly Native Hawaiians, speak Hawaiian as their first language. The census counted 170 people in 2010 and 84 in 2020.
mechanism: A monarch sold the land, and the family has kept it through the change from kingdom to United States rule. Title gives the owners the power to control who enters, but no separate sovereignty.

name: Franco-Texian Bill
aka: Franco Texian Commercial and Colonization Company
anchor: Marker is in central Texas; the land lay in scattered tracts along rivers.
founder: Jean Pierre Hippolyte Basterrèche and Pierre François de Lassaulx
stopped_by: A threatened veto by acting president David Burnet
recognition: A bill before the Texas Congress; never enacted
cost: Three million acres, against 8,000 families, 20 forts and 15 per cent of mine returns
story: The Franco-Texian Bill was a proposal in 1841 for the Republic of Texas, then an independent country, to grant three million acres to a private French company. Two Frenchmen, Basterrèche and de Lassaulx, wanted to set up the Franco Texian Commercial and Colonization Company. It was to bring in 8,000 families and build and keep up 20 forts for 20 years. In return it would receive the land, scattered along Texas rivers, and its settlers would pay no taxes or tariffs for 20 years. It would also get exclusive trade with the New Mexico settlements and could develop mines, paying Texas 15 per cent of gross returns. The French envoy to Texas, Dubois de Saligny, and Sam Houston both supported it, and the House approved it on 23 January 1841. It never reached the Senate, because its sponsors saw they could not get the two-thirds majority needed to overcome a threatened veto by acting president David Burnet, so nothing was ever built.
mechanism: A cash-poor new state offered land and tax freedom to a foreign company in exchange for settlers and defence. It would have remained Texan territory, and the plan failed in the legislature.

sources.t: Franco-Texian Bill, Handbook of Texas Online

name: Poyais
anchor: Marker is on the Mosquito Coast of Honduras; the grant had no surveyed position.
stopped_by: Settlers died or were evacuated; MacGregor retired the scheme in the late 1830s
pop: About 250 settlers, of whom two-thirds died
challenge: Tried for fraud in France and acquitted
cost: £11 for 100 acres; a £200,000 bond and a later £800,000 bond
story: Poyais was a country that did not exist, sold to British investors and settlers in the 1820s by a Scottish adventurer named Gregor MacGregor. MacGregor had fought in the Venezuelan war of independence and briefly seized Amelia Island in Florida. In 1820 he persuaded the Mosquito King, an Indigenous ruler, to grant him about 8 million acres on the Caribbean coast of what is now Honduras. The land was undeveloped jungle. Back in London he called himself the Cazique, or prince, of Poyais and described a prosperous nation with a capital and an opera house, backed by a guidebook, maps and documents that were nearly all fabricated. He sold a £200,000 bond and offered 100 acres of farmland for £11, along with military commissions and government posts. Two ships took about 250 settlers out in 1822 and 1823. They found no capital and no country, only jungle, and malaria and other diseases spread among them until a ship from Belize rescued the survivors in May 1823. Two-thirds of them died. MacGregor moved to Paris and tried again, was tried for fraud there and acquitted for lack of evidence, then sold more bonds and land certificates in London into the 1830s. He died in Venezuela in 1845 and was never convicted.
mechanism: A land grant from a local ruler was the one real element, and the rest was invented. Buyers paid for land and posts in a state that existed only in MacGregor's documents.

sources.t: The Con Man Who Invented His Own Country, History.com

name: Lüderitz's purchase of Angra Pequena
anchor: The town of Lüderitz, at the original anchorage.
stopped_by: He ran out of money and sold to the German Colonial Society
challenge: Frederiks tried to complain to the German government
cost: £100 and 200 rifles, then £500 and 60 rifles; resold for 500,000 marks
story: German South West Africa, now Namibia, began with purchases by a merchant from Bremen, Adolf Lüderitz. In May 1883 he bought the anchorage at Angra Pequena and the land 8 kilometres around it from Josef Frederiks II, a chief of Bethanie, for £100 in gold and 200 rifles. In August he bought a coastal strip between the Orange River and Angra Pequena for £500 and 60 rifles. The second contract gave the width as 20 geographical miles. A German geographical mile is about 7.4 kilometres, while the mile used locally was the English mile of 1.6 kilometres, and both Lüderitz and the missionary who witnessed the deal knew that Frederiks did not understand the difference. He had sold nearly all his people's land. His complaint to the German government was never delivered, because the official carrying it died on the way home, and Germans called the deal the Mile Swindle. Chancellor Otto von Bismarck at first held back, then declared protection when Britain moved to take the coast, and the German flag went up on 7 August 1884. Lüderitz kept buying from other chiefs, but found no gold or diamonds and ran out of money. In April 1885 he sold everything to the German Colonial Society for 500,000 marks, and he died the next year.
mechanism: A merchant's private land deals became the basis for a colony only when his government chose to declare protection over them. A chief sold land under terms he had been misled about, and the German Foreign Office itself later doubted the treaty's validity.

name: Assab Bay and the Rubattino Company
anchor: The port of Assab.
founder: Giuseppe Sapeto for the Rubattino Shipping Company
stopped_by: Taken over by the Italian government in 1882
challenge: Egypt declared the sale illegal
cost: 6,000 Maria Theresa thalers
story: Assab is a port in Eritrea on the Red Sea that started Italy's colony there through a private purchase. In the middle of the 19th century it was an Afar fishing village of about 100 people. On 15 November 1869 an Italian missionary, Giuseppe Sapeto, bought the bay on behalf of the Rubattino Shipping Company from two brothers, the sultans Hasan and Ibrahim ibn Ahmed, for 6,000 Maria Theresa thalers, a silver coin widely used in the region. Sapeto argued that the port was well placed near the Bab-el-Mandeb strait, and that although it was nominally under the sultan of Aussa it was really independent. The press and parliament in Italy opposed the purchase, and Egypt declared the sale illegal. The Italian government took control of the port in 1882, and this led to the colony of Italian Eritrea.
mechanism: A company bought the land and the state later stepped in to hold it. Egypt's protest shows that a sale by local rulers does not settle who has the right to sell.

name: 1819 Singapore Treaty
anchor: The Singapore River area, where the post was set up.
founder: Stamford Raffles for the British East India Company
challenge: Both local signers said they had been forced to agree
cost: 5,000 Spanish dollars a year to the Sultan and 3,000 to the Temenggong
story: The 1819 Singapore Treaty is the agreement that let a British trading company, the East India Company, set up in Singapore, and it is officially treated as the founding of the modern city. The company wanted a base to get around Dutch taxes on shipping in the region, and Stamford Raffles, a company official, won support in India to look for one. Signed on 6 February 1819, the treaty allowed the company to keep a factory, the old word for a trading post, in the lands of Sultan Hussein and Temenggong Abdul Rahman, the local chief. In exchange the company would pay them 5,000 and 3,000 Spanish dollars a year. They also promised not to make a treaty with any other nation or let any other European or American power settle. Soon afterwards both men wrote to the Dutch and others saying they had been forced to sign. On 1 March Britain made them sign a statement of consent, and the Temenggong said his complaint had only been meant to head off Dutch retaliation.
mechanism: The company paid yearly sums for the right to trade and to keep rivals out. This treaty did not buy sovereignty, and it gave Britain its trading post.

name: Sale of the Isle of Man to the Crown
anchor: Marker is at the centre of the island.
stopped_by: Sale to the Crown
challenge: Islanders opposed merging into Cumberland
recognition: Feudal lordship under the British Crown
cost: £70,000 in 1765 for feudal rights; £417,144 in 1828 for remaining rights
story: The Isle of Man, in the Irish Sea, was for a long time a feudal holding of a noble family, which sold its rights to the British government. A 1609 Act of Parliament had given the rights of Lord of Man to the Earl of Derby and his heirs, and they came down to the Dukes of Atholl. Because Parliament had fixed them by law, it took another Act to end them. Under a contract with the British Treasury, Charlotte, Duchess of Atholl, sold the rights to the Crown for £70,000, and the Isle of Man Purchase Act of 1765, also called the Act of Revestment, put this into effect. Plans to merge the island into the English county of Cumberland met fierce local resistance, led by Sir George Moore, Speaker of the House of Keys, a chamber of the island's parliament, and did not go ahead. The family kept its manor rights, its power to choose the bishop and other privileges, and sold those in 1828 for £417,144.
mechanism: Here a state bought ruling rights from a private family. The sale needed an Act of Parliament because an earlier Act had created those rights.

name: Transylvania Purchase
anchor: Marker is in central Kentucky, inside the claimed tract.
stopped_by: The Virginia General Assembly (1778) and North Carolina (1783)
laws: A compact of government agreed by settlers in May 1775
challenge: Voided by Virginia and North Carolina
cost: Goods worth about £10,000 by some estimates
story: The Transylvania Colony was an attempt by a North Carolina judge and land speculator, Richard Henderson, to create a private colony in what is now Kentucky and north central Tennessee. A 1763 British proclamation had forbidden colonial settlement west of the Appalachians, but Henderson's Transylvania Company hoped to get around this by buying the land directly from the Cherokee and winning approval as a British colony owned by its proprietors. In 1775, at Sycamore Shoals, most leading Cherokee chiefs accepted a treaty selling the land for goods that some scholars estimate at about £10,000. Henderson hired Daniel Boone to cut the Wilderness Road through the Cumberland Gap, and in May 1775 settlers agreed a compact of government. Virginia and North Carolina both claimed parts of the same land. The Revolutionary War held back most settlement. The Virginia General Assembly threw out the claim in Kentucky in 1778, and North Carolina threw out the Tennessee portion in 1783. Each compensated Henderson and his partners with a grant of 200,000 acres.
mechanism: Buying from an Indigenous nation gave no title that colonial governments would accept. Virginia and North Carolina voided the claim because they claimed the same land, and paid Henderson off with smaller grants.

name: Johnson v. M'Intosh
anchor: Marker is in Illinois, where the case began.
stopped_by: US Supreme Court
challenge: Unanimous Supreme Court ruling against the private buyers
story: Johnson v. M'Intosh is an 1823 United States Supreme Court case that set the rule on private people buying land from Native American nations. Thomas Johnson, later a Supreme Court justice, had bought land from the Piankeshaw in 1773 and 1775. People claiming through his heirs sued William McIntosh, who held a federal land patent, a government deed, to what they said was the same land. Evidence suggests the two tracts did not actually overlap, and that the parties knew this and misstated the facts to get a ruling. A court in Illinois dismissed the claim because the Piankeshaw could not transfer the land. Chief Justice John Marshall, writing for a unanimous Supreme Court, upheld the dismissal. He set out the doctrine of discovery, under which a European power gained sovereignty over land it discovered, along with the sole right to buy out the Indigenous occupants, who kept only a right to occupy it. The case remains a standard part of American legal teaching and the basis of the law of aboriginal title, the rights Indigenous peoples keep over their land.
mechanism: Private citizens could not buy land from Native American nations, because only the sovereign could acquire it. The rule made the state the only lawful buyer, whatever price or agreement a private person might reach.

name: Batman's Treaty
anchor: A suggested site of the signing, on the Merri Creek; the exact spot is debated.
founder: John Batman for the Port Phillip Association
stopped_by: Governor Bourke's proclamation of 26 August 1835
challenge: Declared void by the Crown
cost: Blankets, tools, clothing and flour for 600,000 acres, with a yearly tribute
story: Batman's Treaty was an 1835 attempt by British colonists to buy the land where Melbourne, Australia, now stands directly from its Aboriginal owners. It is the first and only documented time Europeans negotiated their presence directly with the traditional owners. The Port Phillip Association, a group of graziers based mostly in Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania), wanted new pasture for sheep and sent John Batman across the strait with a deed drawn up by a lawyer. On 6 June he met eight Wurundjeri and Boonwurrung elders. For 600,000 acres he handed over blankets, tomahawks, knives, scissors, looking glasses, handkerchiefs, shirts, clothes and flour, and the deed promised a yearly tribute. On 26 August the Governor of New South Wales, Richard Bourke, proclaimed such agreements void against the rights of the Crown and declared anyone on Crown land without authority a trespasser. The Colonial Office in London approved this in October. Its objections were that Batman had bought from Aboriginal people, whom British colonists did not accept had any claim to land, and that he had bought for the Association instead of the Crown.
mechanism: The Crown treated all land as its own, so a private purchase from the Aboriginal owners had no legal force. The governor cancelled the deal by proclamation.

name: Charles de Thierry's New Zealand claim
anchor: Hokianga Harbour, Northland.
stopped_by: Local chiefs rejected his claim; the Treaty of Waitangi ended it
challenge: Tāmati Wāka Nene and Patuone rejected his claim
cost: 36 axes for 40,000 acres
story: Charles de Thierry, the son of a French family who had fled to England, tried to create his own sovereign state in New Zealand before the Treaty of Waitangi of 1840. While at Cambridge he met Hongi Hika, a Ngāpuhi chief visiting England, and through the missionary Thomas Kendall arranged to buy 40,000 acres at Hokianga, in Northland, for 36 axes. In 1835 he reached the Pacific, announced himself King of Nuku Hiva in the Marquesas Islands, and wrote to the British Resident in New Zealand that he would arrive as sovereign chief. He recruited followers in Sydney in 1837, but on reaching Hokianga the chiefs Tāmati Wāka Nene and Patuone rejected his claims. They allowed him a plot of only 800 acres. His followers rioted and left, and he came to depend on Māori charity. The Treaty of Waitangi between the British Crown and Māori chiefs in 1840 ended any chance of his scheme. He moved to Auckland and taught piano until his death in 1864.
mechanism: A purchase made at long distance through a go-between meant little once the local chiefs said it did not stand. Land use could be granted by those chiefs, but sovereignty did not come with it.

name: Liberia and the American Colonization Society
anchor: Monrovia, near Cape Mesurado.
challenge: Indigenous peoples attacked the settlement
story: Liberia, in West Africa, grew from land acquired by a private American organisation, the American Colonization Society, which raised money to send free Black Americans to Africa. Its first ship left New York in 1820, with agents sent to find a site. In December 1821 they acquired Cape Mesurado, a 36-mile strip near present-day Monrovia, from a local ruler, King Peter, perhaps under some threat of force. The colonists were attacked by the peoples whose territory it was, and suffered from disease and hunger. Only 1,819 of the 4,571 emigrants who arrived between 1820 and 1843 survived. The colony spread along the coast and inland, sometimes by force, and other American colonisation societies set up their own settlements. These joined as the Commonwealth of Liberia in 1838. Under its first Black governor, Joseph Jenkins Roberts, Liberians voted for independence, and they declared it on 26 July 1847. The descendants of the settlers, called Americo-Liberians, controlled the country's politics until 1980.
mechanism: A private society obtained land from a local ruler and governed it as a colony, and the settlers later declared a state. It is a case of a private body's land deal growing into a recognised country, with the colony expanding at times by force against those already living there.

name: Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone
founder: Kings Romans Group and owner Zhao Wei
currency: Chinese yuan and Thai baht are commonly accepted
challenge: US Treasury sanctions in 2018
recognition: Created by the Lao government; remains in Laos
cost: Lease of 10,000 hectares for 99 years; price not given
story: The Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone is a casino and hotel district on the Mekong River in Bokeo Province, Laos, run by a private company on a long lease. In 2007 the Hong Kong-registered Kings Romans Group and the Lao government created the zone to promote development. The company took a 99-year lease on 10,000 hectares, with 3,000 hectares set aside as a duty-free zone. It draws mostly Chinese visitors. Mandarin is widely spoken, the clocks are set to Beijing time and the Chinese yuan is the usual currency, so some have labelled it a Chinese colony in all but name. In January 2018 the United States Treasury imposed sanctions on the company and its owner, Zhao Wei, accusing them of money laundering and of drug, human and animal trafficking. Zhao Wei denies this. Lao authorities have taken some enforcement action, and the zone still operates.
mechanism: A lease of this kind leaves the land in Laos while giving a company wide control of what happens there. No sovereignty passed on paper, though the place operates much like a separate Chinese-speaking territory.

name: Daewoo land deal in Madagascar
anchor: Marker is at the centre of Madagascar; the plots were in the west and the east.
stopped_by: Andry Rajoelina cancelled the deal after taking power in March 2009
challenge: Popular protest
recognition: Agreement with the Madagascar government, later cancelled
cost: $6 billion in promised infrastructure over 20 to 25 years, for use of 1.3 million hectares
story: In 2008 a South Korean company, Daewoo Logistics, agreed with the government of Madagascar to lease 1.3 million hectares of farmland for 99 years, an area larger than Qatar and by one report about half of the island's arable land. South Korea was one of the world's largest buyers of imported corn, and food prices had recently spiked, so Daewoo wanted to grow corn on 1 million hectares in the west and oil palm on 300,000 hectares in the east, for export. It promised to spend $6 billion over 20 to 25 years on roads, railways, a port and schools. Critics said the deal ignored local people's customary use of the land, in a country where many could barely feed themselves. Anger over it helped fuel the movement against President Marc Ravalomanana, who had signed it, and he was driven from office in March 2009. Andry Rajoelina, the 34-year-old mayor of the capital, replaced him and within a day said the deal was off, because the constitution said Madagascar's land was neither for sale nor for rent. A few months later a campaign group, Rainforest Rescue, said Daewoo still held 218,000 hectares. No report says how that claim was resolved.
mechanism: A lease moves land use and leaves sovereignty with the state. The new leader cancelled this one on the ground that the constitution barred selling or renting out land.

sources.t: Madagascar's new leader says Daewoo land deal off, Reuters
Despite violent protests and coup, Daewoo continues to hold cropland in Madagascar, Mongabay

name: Jarch Capital's lease from a warlord's family
anchor: Marker is in southern Sudan near the Nile; the tract's exact position was not given.
challenge: Experts and regional officials doubted the rights could be asserted
cost: Undisclosed, for a 400,000-hectare leasehold
story: In January 2009 Philippe Heilberg, a former Wall Street banker who chaired the New York firm Jarch Capital, said he had secured leasehold rights to 400,000 hectares in south Sudan, an area the size of Dubai. He did it by taking a majority stake in a company controlled by the son of Paulino Matip, a warlord who had fought on both sides of Sudan's civil war and became deputy commander of the southern army after a 2005 peace deal. The Financial Times called it post-colonial Africa's biggest private land deal, second only to Daewoo's in Madagascar. Heilberg refused to say what he paid. He said he was betting that Sudan and possibly other African states would break apart, and that being in early on such shifts in sovereignty would pay off. Land law in the south was unclear, and experts and regional officials doubted he could enforce his rights. South Sudan did become independent in 2011. No report says whether the lease was ever enforced.
mechanism: A private investor bought rights from an armed commander instead of a government, betting that a future state would honour them. Such a deal passes no sovereignty, and its value depends on who ends up ruling.

sources.t: US investor buys Sudanese warlord's land, Financial Times

name: Calls for Greece to sell islands
anchor: Marker is in the Aegean Sea; no specific islands were named.
stopped_by: Rejected by Greece
story: In March 2010, during Greece's debt crisis, two German politicians said the country should sell islands to raise cash. Greece's budget deficit had reached 12.7 per cent of its economy in 2009, against the European Union's limit of 3 per cent, and opinion polls showed Germans strongly against paying to rescue it. The newspaper Bild ran the story under the headline "Sell your islands, you bankrupt Greeks! And sell the Acropolis too!" One of the politicians, Schaeffler, said that a country needing to save money must sell its jewellery, so to speak, and privatise. Greece's deputy foreign minister, Dimitris Droutsas, said such suggestions were not appropriate. The remarks named no buyer and no particular island.
mechanism: A proposal of this kind has no legal effect unless the state that holds the land agrees to sell. Greece dismissed the idea.

sources.t: Greece urged to sell islands, Al Jazeera

name: Tiran and Sanafir transfer
anchor: Tiran Island.
founder: Governments of Egypt and Saudi Arabia
challenge: An Egyptian court ruled against the transfer in January 2017; street protests
recognition: Treaty between Egypt and Saudi Arabia
cost: Critics link it to billions of dollars of Saudi aid; the government says the islands were always Saudi
story: Tiran and Sanafir are two Red Sea islands at the mouth of the Gulf of Aqaba, and Egypt agreed in April 2016 to hand them to Saudi Arabia. Tiran controls the shipping lane to the ports of Eilat in Israel and Aqaba in Jordan, and Egypt's closure of that lane helped cause the 1967 Arab-Israeli war. The Egyptian government says the islands were always Saudi and were put under Egypt's protection in the 1950s because of tensions with Israel. Critics link the transfer to billions of dollars of Saudi aid to the government of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi and call it a sell-off of national territory. The announcement, during a visit by the Saudi king, set off the largest protests against the government since 2014, and hundreds of people were arrested. A court ruled against the transfer in January 2017. Politicians backing it argued that parliament had the right to ratify treaties, and on 14 June 2017, a day after police beat protesters in Cairo, parliament voted to ratify the agreement.
mechanism: Sovereignty was to move by treaty between two states. The Egyptian government calls it the return of Saudi islands and critics call it a sale, and an Egyptian court and parliament came to opposite conclusions.

sources.t: Egypt lawmakers approve island transfer to Saudi Arabia, Al Jazeera

name: Tulagi lease to China Sam
anchor: Tulagi island.
stopped_by: Attorney-General John Muria
challenge: Declared unlawful and unenforceable
story: In September 2019 the provincial government of Central Province in the Solomon Islands signed an agreement giving a Chinese state-linked developer, China Sam Enterprise Group, exclusive development rights to the island of Tulagi and its neighbours. RNZ, the New Zealand public broadcaster, described it as a five-year lease deal. It came around the time the Solomon Islands opened diplomatic relations with China. The agreement spoke vaguely of trade, minerals, possible oil and gas, and a special economic zone. Local people and Western diplomats were alarmed, and one senior diplomat said that the wording could allow strategic assets such as deep-sea ports. In October the national Attorney-General, John Muria, said it was unlawful and unenforceable and must be terminated at once. It had not been vetted by his office as the law required, and an illegal clause would have exempted the company from foreign-investor rules. The provincial premier, Stanley Manetiva, said the deal was not legally binding and was no longer an issue.
mechanism: The Attorney-General ordered this provincial agreement ended because it skipped the review required for such deals and tried to exempt the investor from national foreign-investment rules.

sources.t: Solomons' AG orders Central Province to 'terminate' China deal, RNZ

name: Douglas Tompkins's land in Chile and Argentina
anchor: Pumalín Park, Chile.
challenge: Chilean parliament, military and senators raised sovereignty objections; 1996 agreement with President Frei
recognition: Private land under Chilean and Argentine sovereignty
story: Douglas Tompkins, the American who founded the clothing firms The North Face and Esprit, spent about three decades buying more than a million hectares of Chile and Argentina to create private nature reserves. He moved to southern Chile after leaving business in 1990 and used go-betweens to buy parcels in Chaitén province, to avoid attention and rising prices. In 1994 he announced Pumalín Park, 275,000 hectares running from the Pacific Ocean to the Argentine border, which in effect cut Chile in two. Chile had recently come out of dictatorship and had nearly gone to war with Argentina over this frontier, so parliament debated whether he was undermining national sovereignty. The military and Patagonian senators objected, and small farmers without land titles said he ignored their rights. In 1996 he agreed with President Frei to stop buying land and to allow infrastructure across it. That agreement was later cancelled by both sides, and he more than doubled his Chilean holdings and bought more in Argentina. He promised to give all the land to the state, but distrust had limited his donations when he died in a kayaking accident in December 2015.
mechanism: Tompkins bought private title while Chile and Argentina kept sovereignty. Chile's politicians still treated one foreign owner's control of a strip from the coast to the border as a question of national territory.

sources.t: Douglas Tompkins: can billionaires really save nature with cold, hard cash?, The Conversation

name: Benetton in Patagonia
anchor: The Leleque ranch, Chubut.
challenge: Mapuche occupations of Santa Rosa in 2002 and 2007; a civil court ruled for Benetton
story: The Italian clothing group Benetton is the largest private landowner in Argentina, holding about 970,000 hectares in Patagonia since it bought the Compañía de Tierras Sud Argentino in 1991. That company dates from 1889, when the Argentine government gave land to 10 British citizens, 90,000 hectares each, passing over the Mapuche people who lived there, many of whom ended up as labourers on the new ranches. In 2002 a Mapuche couple, Atilio Curiñanco and Rosa Nahuelquir, moved with their children onto Santa Rosa, a 534-hectare part of the Leleque ranch, believing it was government land. The company complained, and police removed them and destroyed their home and crops. A judge cleared them of criminal blame, but ruled in the civil case that the land was Benetton's. In 2004 they travelled to Rome with the Nobel Peace laureate Adolfo Pérez Esquivel to meet Luciano Benetton, who promised to look for a solution. He offered the Chubut provincial government 7,500 hectares elsewhere for Mapuche farming, and the province rejected it as unproductive. In February 2007, 25 Mapuche including six families occupied Santa Rosa again, saying it was their ancestral territory. No report says how that occupation ended.
mechanism: The purchase gave the company title under Argentine law, and that title traces to an 1889 state grant made without the consent of the Mapuche. Land changed hands, sovereignty did not, and Argentine courts have treated the title as valid.

sources.t: Argentina: Mapuches Return to Benetton-Held Land, Inter Press Service

name: Trump statement on buying Gaza
anchor: Gaza City area.
challenge: Rejected by Hamas
story: On 9 February 2025, President Donald Trump told reporters on Air Force One, "I'm committed to buying and owning Gaza," referring to the Palestinian coastal territory devastated by war. He said other Middle Eastern states might rebuild sections under American auspices and that the United States would make sure Hamas did not move back. He had also spoken of permanently moving Palestinians out to create a "Riviera of the Middle East". His remarks named no seller and no price. Ezzat El Rashq of the Hamas political bureau answered that "Gaza is not a property to be sold and bought" and said Palestinians would defeat any displacement plans.
mechanism: A purchase needs a seller with the power to transfer the land. The statement named none, and Hamas rejected the idea of a sale.

sources.t: I am committed to buying and owning Gaza, says Trump, Gulf Today

name: Satoshi Island
anchor: Marker is off the east coast of Santo, Vanuatu; position estimated.
stopped_by: Breach of the land lease
passports: Tokens described as citizenship; Vanuatu gave no such status
cost: About €100,000 to €120,000 for a home package, according to press reports
story: Satoshi Island was a plan to turn a private island in Vanuatu, in the South Pacific, into a smart city for cryptocurrency users. Lataro Island is about 3.2 square kilometres of mostly rainforest, and a British entrepreneur, Anthony Welch, had lived there since 2007 under a 75-year lease. In 2022 he announced that he would sell plots as NFTs, digital tokens recorded on a blockchain, and aimed at a community of more than 20,000 people in modular homes. The project's material spoke of private ownership and citizenship, but the writer Raymond Craib pointed out that "citizenship" meant owning one of 21,000 tokens, and buyers would still need a passport to enter Vanuatu. Vanuatu's government said a token gave no right of residence. The project claimed about 50,000 people had invested, a figure repeated in press reports and not independently confirmed. In July 2025 the company behind it, Satoshi Island DAO LLC, said all its digital assets could no longer be traded because of a breach of the land lease, citing no real development, no money to keep the site safe and no benefit to local people. There is no clear evidence that any housing unit was delivered, and its website has gone offline.
mechanism: Welch held only a lease under Vanuatu law, so token buyers received neither land ownership nor citizenship. The project ended over a breach of that lease.

sources.t: Crypto Bros Are Trying to Buy an Island in the Pacific, Jacobin
50,000 people paid to live on the Bitcoin Island, MeinMMO

name: Herzl's offer to the Ottoman Sultan for Palestine
anchor: Marker is at Jerusalem, in Ottoman Palestine.
stopped_by: Sultan Abdul Hamid II refused
cost: £20 million offered in 1896, according to one historical account
story: Theodor Herzl, one of the founders of Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, tried in 1896 and 1901 to get Palestine from the Ottoman Empire, which ruled it and was deeply in debt to European powers. According to an account published by the Turkish public broadcaster TRT World, he offered £20 million in 1896 for a charter allowing Jews to settle there, using intermediaries named Philip de Newlinski and Arminius Vambery. Sultan Abdul Hamid II refused, telling Newlinski that he could not sell a foot of land because it belonged to his people, who had won it with their blood. Herzl met the sultan in person in 1901 and proposed a company of Jewish financiers in Istanbul that would buy up Ottoman debt over time, in return for autonomy for some land in Palestine as a destination for Jewish migrants. The sultan was interested in consolidating the debt but treated it as a separate matter from settlement, so nothing came of the land proposal.
mechanism: Part of a state can be sold only if its ruler agrees, and the sultan refused even while in debt. Herzl's later plan offered debt relief as the price and asked for autonomy instead of full sovereignty.

sources.t: How Theodor Herzl failed to convince the Ottomans to sell Palestine, TRT World
